data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense of the preference for corroborated theories is structurally underdetermined and circular. It claims the preference is defensible as a constitutive rule because 'without it, the game of science (conjecture and refutation) stops' and rests on 'no deeper logical ground than the desire to play the game.' But this argument cannot single out corroboration specifically. Infinitely many alternative constitutive rules would also sustain a recognizable game of conjecture and refutation — e.g., preferring the least-corroborated theory, preferring theories alphabetically, or preferring theories at random. Each of these would equally 'keep a game going,' and each would rest on the same bare 'desire to play.' The target provides no criterion within its own framework that discriminates the corroboration rule from these rivals, so its defense collapses into mere stipulation. Worse, the argument is circular: the game of science is defined to include the corroboration rule, so removing any defining rule trivially 'stops the game' — but that tells us nothing about why this rule rather than another deserves constitutive status. The target's own countercondition ('If a constitutive rule must itself be justified by external criteria to be rational') is acknowledged but left entirely unaddressed, which concedes the gap without closing it.
